We spent years optimizing LinkedIn for reactions and follower count, and two new studies show those numbers barely predict whether AI tools cite your post. ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI mode now reference LinkedIn in 11% of their answers, so your buyers are reading 
LinkedIn posts inside AI search whether or not you ever go viral. Accounts under 500 followers get cited at the same rate as accounts with tens of thousands, which means audience size is no longer the gating factor.

This video covers what actually gets your LinkedIn content cited by AI, based on Semrush's analysis of 89,000 LinkedIn URLs and Scrunch's analysis of 12,000 posts. It breaks down the three patterns that drive citations (technical details at +77%, named entities at +33%, topic specificity at +18%), the two formatting choices that quietly kill your odds (Unicode characters at -58% and link-in-comments at -31% for the post), and the Two-Surface Play with LinkedIn articles that almost no founder is running yet. 

You will also see a real example from Neza, a battery safety consultant who landed a paid training project after an agency found her through AI search.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
 Why LinkedIn is now the #2 most cited source in AI search
 The reaction count myth and why 15 reactions can outrank 10,000
 Why accounts under 500 followers get cited at the same rate
 The three content patterns that drive AI citations
 The Unicode formatting trap that makes your profile invisible to ChatGPT
 When link-in-comments helps you and when it costs you
 The Two-Surface Play: turning blog posts into LinkedIn articles
 The 5-step plan to make your content AI-citable this week

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
 LinkedIn is the second most cited domain across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI mode
 Reaction count has near zero predictive power on whether AI cites a post
 The median cited LinkedIn post has 15 to 25 reactions and one comment
 Technical details, meaning specific numbers, tools, and real data, raise citation rate by 77%
 Unicode bold and italic formatting drops ChatGPT citation rate by 58% and can hide your entire profile
 LinkedIn articles account for 50 to 66% of all cited LinkedIn content, and almost no one is publishing them
